Header:
Date: 2026-03-10
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Alex Monroe (Solstice CTO), Priya Singh (Solstice Eng), Derek Wu (Solstice Product)

Summary (auto): quick SDK walkthrough for Python and TypeScript, auth options (API key vs SSO), environment setup, and quickstarts; discuss hosted vs dedicated for latency/cost, verify security needs and next steps to run bench test.

Topics: SDK quickstarts, auth, env vars, streaming, webhooks, Dedicated vs Hosted, Private/VPC, security docs, bench testing

00:00 Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick intro, i'm jordan from redwood inference, this is priya our se.
00:07 Alex: hey thanks, alex here, i'll let the team jump in after, thanks for doing this, we wanted to see how fast integration looks for our devs.
00:15 Priya (SE): cool, our plan is short walkthrough: python + typescript quickstarts, auth patterns, then show console and optimize briefly, then q and a. sound good?
00:22 Alex: yep perfect.
00:30 Priya (SE): ok starting with python, there's two main flows: simple hosted api with an api key, or dedicated/private where you get a private endpoint and options for sso/kms. for quickstarts we usually show pip install redwood-sdk, set REDWOOD_API_KEY env var, then minimal call to client.generate.
00:52 Priya S. (Cust): do you have an official package name? our infra folks need it for audits.
00:58 Priya (SE): yeah, it's redwood-inference for python, and @redwood/inference for node/ts; docs link in the quickstart. note: some transcribes sometimes show it as 'redwood-infer' but the actual package is redwood-inference.
01:12 Derek: how is auth handled for dedicated? do we still use api keys?
01:18 Priya (SE): good q — dedicated supports both api keys and mTLS + jwt-based SSO. enterprise customers often do SAML + SSO to provision short-lived tokens via the private control plane; we also integrate with KMS for key wrapping if you need customer-managed keys.
01:36 Alex: any differences in SDK code? or just endpoint + key?
01:40 Priya (SE): mostly endpoint + token. the SDK accepts a base_url override plus a token provider. for node we show an example using a credential provider function that refreshes tokens from your idp. python example uses requests auth hook or the SDK's built-in token callback.
01:55 Jordan: i'll screen-share the quickstart repo — bear with me while i switch screens.
02:10 [screen share noise, typing]
02:25 Priya (SE): here is the python quickstart. Step 1: pip install redwood-inference. Step 2: export REDWOOD_API_KEY="<key>". Step 3: from redwood import Client; client = Client(); client.generate("Write a summary..."). For streaming we do client.stream_generate and handle chunk callbacks.
02:48 Priya S. (Cust): streaming — is that server-sent events or websockets?
02:52 Priya (SE): currently we offer streaming over HTTP/2 chunked responses and websockets in the private runtime; the SDK abstracts both. small note: some customers saw flaky proxy behaviors with websockets behind their corp proxies, we recommend http/2 chunked in those environments.
03:12 Alex: ok, typescript example?
03:15 Priya (SE): node example: npm i @redwood/inference; import {Client} from '@redwood/inference'; const c = new Client({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const resp = await c.generate({ model: 'redwood-v1', prompt: '...' });
03:33 Alex: can you do function/tool calling with the sdk? we have some tool orchestration already.
03:38 Priya (SE): yes, function calling is supported. we serialize tool specs in the call, the sdk will surface structured output. note: older transcripts sometimes say 'tool calling' as 'tul calling' — it's function calling.
03:50 Derek: latency concerns — we're considering a 99th percentile SLO of 200ms for short chat use cases. what are the realistic numbers?
03:58 Priya (SE): with hosted small models you can get ~100-200ms for single-token step but it depends a lot on batch size and sequence lengths. Dedicated on-prem with pinned GPUs will be more stable — you'll hit lower variance. Also caching (prefix/KV cache) helps; sometimes the transcript call it 'kv cash' which is the same.
04:18 Alex: cost tradeoffs?
04:21 Priya (SE): batching reduces per-token cost, but increases p95 latency. Our Optimize tool suggests batching configs per route and estimates unit cost savings. For your 200ms SLO we can set batch thresholds low and use smaller batch windows; Dedicated gives more predictable throughput cost.
04:40 Alex: security — SOC2 and data residency — we operate in eu for some customers.
04:45 Jordan: we have SOC 2 and ISO docs; for data residency we support region pinning and private deployments. i'll attach the security whitepaper. we also support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM.
04:58 Priya S.: what about audit logs and RBAC?
05:02 Priya (SE): console exposes per-token cost/latency, traces, and an audit log stream; RBAC integrates with SSO. we'll share sample console screenshots.
05:18 Jordan: quick demo of console — switching windows — this shows routes, model pinning, rollout canaries, and the optimize suggestions panel.
05:40 [screen noise]
05:55 Priya (SE): important for integration: env vars vs secrets manager. we recommend storing keys in vault or cloud secret manager and referencing them in CI; do not hardcode keys. for short-lived tokens use the token provider and refresh it.
06:15 Derek: our infra uses vault and kubernetes secrets — ok?
06:18 Priya (SE): yes, that's common. the sdk supports reading from file or env; in k8s we recommend mounting secrets as env vars or using a sidecar token refresher.
06:30 Alex: one more question — offline/on-prem package? we have regulated customers who need air-gapped installs.
06:36 Priya (SE): we have a private deployment package for on-prem that includes the control plane you can host; it contains the runtime, and we've done air-gapped installs before. note that hardware procurement (GPUs) is on the customer side for on-prem.
06:50 Alex: great. can we run a small pilot to validate latency and cost?
06:53 Jordan: absolutely. typical pilot: 2-4 week POC on dev traffic, we provision Dedicated sandbox or a hosted test with higher limits, you run bench tests and share traces. our SE team will help with the bench harness.
07:06 Priya S.: what's the bench harness look like?
07:09 Priya (SE): we share a small load generator and a spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99 token counts, prompt length distributions, and sample payloads. we can also run a joint run where we capture traces and token metrics.
07:24 Alex: ok that sounds good.
07:28 Jordan: quick note on SDK versions: we're on 1.x stable for core features; some of the newer optimize APIs are in 1.2/1.3 and labelled experimental. we'll call those out in the docs.
07:42 Derek: any known issues for node in older proxies?
07:45 Priya (SE): yeah proxies sometimes block websockets; use http2 chunked streaming or fallback to polling. we captured that in the troubleshooting section.
07:58 Alex: competitors — we evaluated openai and anthorpic; curious about model options you provide.
08:05 Priya (SE): we host a model catalog with curated open models and redwood-verified performance profiles; you can pick smaller quantized variants for cost savings. Optimize suggests quantization levels per workload.
08:22 Alex: ok next steps?
08:25 Jordan: recap — we'll send: (1) quickstart links (python/typescript) with sample repos, (2) sandbox api keys and instructions (Priya to provision), (3) SOC2 + security whitepaper and data residency notes, (4) pricing + Dedicated options, (5) bench harness and example prompts.
08:45 Priya S.: can you include a sample token budget estimation?
08:49 Jordan: yes we'll include a simple token cost calc spreadsheet.
08:53 Alex: timeline — we want to start pilot next week if possible.
08:57 Jordan: we'll aim to have keys and docs in 48 hours.
09:02 [wrap up]
09:10 Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the deck and artifacts.
09:15 Alex: thanks all.
